main:
Breeze of Breslov

Parashas Tetzaveh | Feb 12th 2022

“Dear Brother, Hold On” 

Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

In the beginning of Parashat Tetzaveh, HaShem instructs Moshe to encourage the Jewish People to bring to him “pure, pressed olive oil for lighting” (Shemot 27:20). All the pristine oil that Moshe gathered would then be used to illuminate the Menorah in the form of a “ner tamid,” a perpetual lighting. This unique luminary in the Mishkan would serve as the model and prototype for the beacon of light which would shine forth from the Beit HaMikdash to the entire world (Menachot 86B). 

Paradoxically, the process of unearthing this potent, ethereal light begins with tremendous pressure and weight placed on the physical olives themselves. Through intense duress alone, the olives then give birth to a wondrous oil capable of brilliant illumination. 

This entire paradigm alludes to the deep, internal process of a Jewish person drawing out the inner light stored within him or herself in order to provide illumination for those all around, and in turn, becoming a “light unto the nations” (Yeshaya 49:6). The goal and destination of a Jew is certainly wondrous, but the path to lighting up one’s brethren is nonetheless preceded by an intense experience of being “katit,” crushed. 

As Chazal famously teach, “Why are the Jews compared to olives? The olive sits upon its branch. It is plucked, squeezed, ground, and crushed, and only then does it give its oil. So too, when the Jews endure suffering, they show their mettle” (Shemot Rabbat 36:1). What allows a person the strength and inner fortitude to endure such intense trials and tribulations on their journey to fulfilling their unique potential? 

In my favorite lesson of Likutey Moharan known in Breslov circles as “The Rebbe’s Letter,” Rebbe Nachman unusually and quite forwardly addresses his students, both in the present and to us now in the future, in the first person. The lesson is reminiscent of a letter written to a dear friend. Here, Rebbe Nachman exhorts each and every one of us in our uniquely challenging path towards actualizing one’s innermost self with these potent words, “When a person begins serving HaShem, the way is that they show him rejection. It seems as if HaShem is completely ignoring him and not turning to him at all because HaShem does not want him at all.

A person needs to be very stubborn, encouraging himself very, very much and paying no attention whatsoever to all this, for in truth, all distancing is nothing but being brought near. A person needs tremendous determination to be strong and courageous, to hold on and maintain his position even if they cause him to fall time and again. This is because one must surely experience all these falls, descents, confusions, and so on before entering the gates of holiness. The True Tzaddikim underwent all this. And so we heard from a True Tzaddik who said: “Had anyone, no matter whom, told me when I first began serving HaShem: “Brother! Be strong and hold on!” I would have run very quick in serving HaShem. For (that Tzaddik) too, experienced all the aforementioned, yet did not hear any encouragement, from anybody. Remember this well! Give yourself much encouragement, and do what you can in serving HaShem. Then, with the accruement of days and years, with HaShem’s help, you will surely enter into the gates of holiness. For HaShem is full of compassion and wants you very much. And so the rule my beloved brother, is to be very strong and courageous” (Likutey Moharan Tinyana, 48). 

The True Tzaddik whom Rebbe Nachman is mysteriously alluding to appears to be himself. But the open ended nature of Rebbe Nachman’s disclaimer lends itself to interpreting these very words to ourselves as well. This is supported by the fact that Rebbe Nachman strongly asserted that anyone who had the courage to be his faithful disciple, without veering even the slightest bit from his established path, would become a great Tzaddik in his own right, come what may (Chayei Moharan, 320). 

Over the course of my years since becoming Ba’al Teshuva and, with HaShem’s compassion, ultimately finding the Rebbe who so deeply resonated with the root of my soul, I have repeatedly drawn tremendous encouragement and inspiration from this letter. Continuously overcoming debilitating mental health conditions and psycho-spiritual vulnerabilities in order to provide light to my family and friends around me has proven to be the most formidable task of my life. And yet, the oil which has been produced by the constant “crushing,” has become a blazing fire of hope and consolation for those around me. This is my pride and joy in both this world and the next. All of this is in merit of my “Moshe Rabbeinu,” the Tzaddik Yesod Olam, Rebbe Nachman, from whom all this oil has been excavated by and gathered to. 

I know I have stated this many times. But I will continue to do so, because this point requires constant encouragement. Do not ever give up. If you fall down, force yourself with whatever means necessary to dust yourself off and get back up again. Even if you fall many times throughout a day, find the courage to start over again. And even if you feel that you are alone in your struggles, you must know that I am over here fighting the very same fight with you. 

And remember, each time you force yourself to begin anew, you are drawing out more and more pure oil. It is this sacred oil which will serve as the primary source of light in the final Beit HaMikdash, a brilliant luminance which will light up the whole world. A real and everlasting “ner tamid.” In the meantime, my dear brother, hold on. 

Shabbat Shalom.
